patient.chief_complaint: Witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure preceded by a rising sensation from the stomach and a feeling of deja vu, with post-ictal inability to speak clearly
patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. Novak is a 33-year-old right-handed graphic designer who presents to the emergency department after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home. His partner reports that approximately four hours prior to arrival, the patient suddenly stopped mid-sentence, stared blankly, and began performing repetitive lip-smacking and chewing movements. His right hand assumed a stiff, bent-wrist posture that the partner describes as resembling a clenched fist held up and twisted inward. He did not respond when called. After approximately 20 to 25 seconds, his entire body stiffened and he fell from the couch onto the floor, developing rhythmic jerking of all four extremities lasting roughly 90 seconds. He was incontinent of urine. Emergency medical services were called. Following the convulsion, the patient was unable to produce coherent speech for approximately five minutes, using jumbled words, before gradually recovering fluency. He was confused and drowsy for a further 25 minutes.

On interview, the patient recalls experiencing an intense wave of nausea rising from his epigastrium toward his throat, immediately followed by an overwhelming and distressing feeling of deja vu, just before losing awareness. He reports having had strikingly similar brief episodes — the rising stomach sensation and deja vu, each lasting 30 to 60 seconds — approximately three to four times per month over the past nine months. He never progressed to convulsive activity during these previous events and remained able to function afterward, though he felt briefly confused and worn out. He discussed one of these episodes with a colleague who suggested it sounded like a panic attack from work stress; a second episode occurring while walking to a coffee shop three years ago had been attributed by the patient himself to low blood sugar and was not reported to any physician.

On two occasions in the last two months, his partner witnessed him stare blankly, smack his lips, and reach at his shirt with his right hand for roughly half a minute, during which he did not respond. He denies prior convulsions aside from the febrile seizure in infancy. There is no recent head trauma, fever, or illness. No prior antiepileptic medications. Sleep has been normal.

results.title: Operational classification of seizure types by the International League Against Epilepsy
results.summary: ILAE 2017 classification categorizes seizures as focal-onset (with or without impaired awareness, with or without focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic progression) or generalized-onset. Focal seizures with temporal lobe aura (epigastric sensation, deja vu) and behavioral arrest with oroalimentary automatisms are classified as focal impaired-awareness seizures. Epilepsy diagnosis requires two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart, one unprovoked seizure with at least 60% recurrence risk over 10 years, or an epilepsy syndrome diagnosis.

results.title: ILAE evidence-based guideline: initial monotherapy for epileptic seizures
results.summary: For adults with new-onset focal epilepsy, levetiracetam and zonisamide have level A evidence; lamotrigine and carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine are level C (possibly effective). Enzyme-inducing AEDs (carbamazepine, phenytoin, oxcarbazepine) have pharmacokinetic interaction potential. Non-enzyme-inducing options (levetiracetam, lamotrigine, lacosamide) are preferred when drug-drug interactions are a concern.

results.title: Practice parameter: evaluating an apparent unprovoked first seizure in adults
results.summary: After a first unprovoked seizure, the 10-year recurrence risk is 21-45%; the presence of a brain lesion (structural MRI abnormality) or an abnormal EEG increases recurrence risk to 65% or higher, meeting ILAE threshold for epilepsy diagnosis after a single event.

output.summary: ILAE 2017 classification supports diagnosing epilepsy after a single unprovoked seizure when brain imaging shows a structural lesion and the EEG is abnormal, as both factors independently elevate 10-year recurrence risk above 60%. First-line monotherapy options for focal epilepsy in adults include levetiracetam (level A), lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine, and lacosamide. Non-enzyme-inducing agents are preferred to minimize pharmacokinetic interactions.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Focal epilepsy of left mesial temporal lobe origin (hippocampal sclerosis)

differential.diagnosis: Focal epilepsy of left temporal lobe origin — other structural cause (low-grade tumor, cavernoma, FCD)
differential.key_features: MRI epilepsy protocol demonstrates classical hippocampal sclerosis morphology with no discrete mass, enhancement, or FCD; structural alternatives excluded by imaging.
Epigastric aura with deja vu, oroalimentary automatisms, and concordant left anterior temporal EEG focus argue strongly against frontal-lobe origin.
Stereotyped aura, witnessed automatisms with contralateral dystonic posturing, post-ictal dysphasia, and EEG abnormalities are not consistent with PNES.
No prodromal lightheadedness or postural trigger; prolonged post-ictal confusion and focal aura exclude cardiac syncope.

differential.diagnosis: Migraine with aura (deja vu / epigastric aura variant)
differential.key_features: Migraine aura does not produce behavioral arrest with automatisms or progress to a tonic-clonic seizure with post-ictal dysphasia.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain detailed seizure history including semiology, aura type, automatism laterality, presence of contralateral dystonic posturing, duration, frequency, post-ictal features (particularly dysphasia), and witness accounts.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Stereotyped focal impaired-awareness seizures with epigastric aura, deja vu, oroalimentary automatisms, right-hand dystonia, and post-ictal language difficulty — localizing to left mesial temporal lobe.

optimal_actions.action: Perform complete neurological examination, including language assessment for subtle inter-ictal anomia or word-finding difficulty indicating left (dominant) hemisphere involvement.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Interictal exam near-normal; mild anomia on confrontation may be present in dominant-hemisphere TLE.

optimal_actions.action: Order routine EEG to identify interictal epileptiform discharges and focal slowing; pursue prolonged or sleep-deprived EEG if routine is non-diagnostic.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Interictal sharp-and-slow-wave discharges and TIRDA in the left anterior temporal region (F7/T3).

optimal_actions.action: Order MRI brain with dedicated epilepsy protocol (3T; thin-cut coronal T1, FLAIR, T2 perpendicular to hippocampal long axis, DWI, SWI, post-gadolinium) to identify hippocampal sclerosis or alternative structural lesion.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Left hippocampal sclerosis with volume loss and T2/FLAIR hyperintensity; no mass, FCD, cavernoma, or dual pathology.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, prolactin (if drawn within 10-20 minutes of the event), and AED levels if on therapy.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Exclude metabolic seizure provocation; prolactin elevation supports recent convulsive seizure; baseline organ function for AED selection.

optimal_actions.action: Search current literature for ILAE epilepsy classification criteria, AED selection for focal epilepsy, and recurrence risk after a single unprovoked seizure with structural MRI lesion.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Evidence supporting epilepsy diagnosis after single seizure with structural lesion + abnormal EEG (>60% recurrence risk); first-line AED options (levetiracetam, lamotrigine, lacosamide, oxcarbazepine).

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions before initiating AED therapy, particularly regarding enzyme induction and any CNS-active comedications.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Non-enzyme-inducing AEDs (levetiracetam, lamotrigine, lacosamide) have minimal interactions; enzyme inducers (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine) carry pharmacokinetic interaction potential.

optimal_actions.action: Pursue prolonged video-EEG monitoring to capture ictal events, confirm left anterior temporal onset, and evaluate surgical candidacy if AED therapy fails.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Habitual seizures with left anterior temporal F7/T3 electrographic onset; ictal semiology including right-hand dystonic posturing and post-ictal dysphasia confirms dominant-hemisphere focus.

optimal_actions.action: Order neuropsychological battery to lateralize memory function, assess verbal memory and naming for surgical risk stratification.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Left-lateralized material-specific verbal memory deficit (impaired CVLT-II) with relatively preserved visual memory — consistent with left mesial temporal dysfunction; important for surgical counseling.

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical features of CNS infection, encephalitis, or immunocompromise; lumbar puncture is not indicated in the routine workup of focal epilepsy with a structural lesion.
No syncope-versus-seizure question and no structural cardiac concern; echocardiogram contributes nothing to the epilepsy evaluation.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is reserved for syncope-versus-seizure differentiation; the focal aura and automatism semiology make cardiac arrhythmia implausible.
Head CT is inferior to MRI for detecting hippocampal sclerosis, FCD, and low-grade tumors, and adds ionizing radiation without diagnostic yield in this context.

sequence_constraints.reason: Structural etiology on MRI (hippocampal sclerosis vs low-grade tumor vs FCD) influences AED selection; MRI result should be known before finalizing the drug interaction check and AED choice.

critical_actions: Recognize the epigastric rising aura with deja vu as classic mesial temporal lobe aura and interpret contralateral (right-hand) dystonic posturing as a reliable lateralizing sign pointing to the left hemisphere focus.
Recognize post-ictal dysphasia as a dominant (left) hemisphere lateralizing sign consistent with a left temporal focus.
Obtain MRI with dedicated epilepsy protocol — a standard brain MRI may miss hippocampal sclerosis; thin coronal cuts perpendicular to the hippocampal axis are required.
Initiate first-line AED appropriate for focal epilepsy (levetiracetam, lamotrigine, oxcarbazepine, or lacosamide) after MRI confirms the structural substrate.
Counsel patient on driving restrictions per state law and seizure-safety precautions.

Recognize that prior episodic events attributed to stress or low blood sugar represent the same stereotyped focal seizures — ILAE epilepsy diagnosis criteria are met given the structural lesion plus recurrent unprovoked events.
contraindicated_actions: Do not exclude temporal lobe epilepsy on the basis of a single normal routine EEG — interictal EEG sensitivity is 25-50% for a single recording; repeat or sleep-deprived EEG improves yield.
Do not perform lumbar puncture without specific clinical indication for CNS infection or encephalitis.
Do not start sodium valproate as first-line monotherapy for confirmed focal epilepsy when levetiracetam, lamotrigine, or lacosamide are available and better tolerated.
Do not attribute post-ictal aphasia to a stroke without allowing 15-30 minutes for resolution and confirming normal brain MRI DWI.
key_reasoning_points: Concordant lateralization: left anterior temporal sharp-and-slow-wave discharges on EEG, left hippocampal sclerosis on epilepsy-protocol MRI, and right-hand dystonic posturing plus post-ictal dysphasia (contralateral/dominant hemisphere signs) all point to a single left mesial temporal focus — the hallmark of high-confidence localization.

Hippocampal sclerosis (T2/FLAIR hyperintensity + volume loss on epilepsy-protocol MRI) is the most common identifiable substrate for mesial temporal lobe epilepsy; childhood febrile seizure history is a classic precipitating factor.

ILAE 2017 epilepsy diagnosis is established after a single unprovoked seizure when a structural brain lesion (hippocampal sclerosis) is present and the EEG is abnormal, both conferring at least 60% 10-year recurrence risk.

Single routine EEG sensitivity is only 25-50% for TLE; a negative or equivocal first recording must not terminate the epilepsy workup — sleep-deprived or prolonged video-EEG is the appropriate next step.
Post-ictal dysphasia is a reliable dominant (left) hemisphere lateralizing sign that should be actively sought in the post-ictal history, as it is highly specific for left TLE.

red_herrings.data_point: A single episode approximately three years prior to presentation attributed by the patient to low blood sugar while walking to a coffee shop, never reported to a physician.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Dismiss the prior event as a non-epileptic episode (hypoglycemic or other) and count only the current convulsion, potentially delaying the epilepsy diagnosis or framing this as a first seizure.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The three-year-old episode was stereotypically identical to the established focal seizure pattern (same prodrome); it represents an earlier unprovoked focal seizure, confirming recurrence and a long untreated seizure disorder rather than an isolated first event.
